$comment: Single source of truth for the poop color chart. Consumed by src/pages/poop-color-chart.astro and by scripts/generate-images.mjs when rendering the shareable PNG.

colors.name: Medium Brown
colors.meaning: Normal. Bile pigment plus healthy transit time.
colors.detail: This is the target. Bile starts out green in the liver, and gut bacteria break it down into stercobilin during a normal 24–72 hour transit — which is what makes stool brown. Consistent medium brown means your bile flow and transit time are both working.

colors.name: Light Brown / Tan
colors.meaning: Usually normal. Often a higher-fiber or higher-dairy diet.
colors.detail: A lighter shade is usually diet, not disease — high fiber intake bulks and lightens stool, and so does a dairy-heavy day. If it drifts toward pale gray or clay and stays there, treat it as the pale category instead.

colors.name: Dark Brown
colors.meaning: Normal. Slower transit, iron supplements, or darker foods.
colors.detail: Longer time in the colon means more water reabsorbed and more pigment concentration. Iron supplements, red wine, dark chocolate and heavily pigmented foods all darken stool. Dark brown is fine; genuinely black and tarry is not.

colors.name: Green
colors.meaning: Fast transit, leafy greens, or food coloring. Usually harmless.
colors.detail: Green usually means bile didn't get the full transit time it needed to break down to brown — so it is most often a speed problem, not a disease. Spinach, kale, matcha, blue or green food dye, and iron supplements also do it. Persistent green with diarrhea is worth a conversation.

colors.name: Yellow / Greasy
colors.meaning: Possible fat malabsorption. Persistent + floating: see a doctor.
colors.detail: Yellow, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats and leaves a film is called steatorrhea, and it means fat is passing through undigested. Occasional episodes follow a very fatty meal. A persistent pattern is associated with celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency and giardia — get it evaluated.

colors.name: Pale / Clay
colors.meaning: Possible bile duct or liver issue. Get this checked.
colors.detail: Stool is brown because of bile. Pale, chalky or clay-colored stool suggests bile isn't reaching the intestine — which can point to a blocked bile duct, gallstones, hepatitis or a pancreatic problem. This is one of the few stool colors that warrants a prompt appointment even without other symptoms, especially alongside dark urine or yellowing skin.

colors.name: Red
colors.meaning: Beets can do this. So can lower-GI bleeding. Rule it out.
colors.detail: Beets, tomato, cranberry and red dye are common and harmless causes. But red also means fresh blood from the lower GI tract — hemorrhoids and fissures most often, and less commonly polyps, IBD or colorectal cancer. If you haven't eaten anything red, or it repeats, get it checked rather than assuming.

colors.name: Black / Tarry
colors.meaning: Iron or bismuth — or upper-GI bleeding. Seek care promptly.
colors.detail: Iron supplements, bismuth (Pepto-Bismol), black licorice and activated charcoal all turn stool black harmlessly. The concerning version is melena: black, sticky, tar-like stool with a distinctive strong smell, which is digested blood from an upper-GI bleed. If you aren't taking iron or bismuth, treat black tarry stool as urgent.
